record.paper_title: Open problems in Euclidean Ramsey Theory
record.original_question: What is the polychromatic number of the Euclidean plane, defined as the least number of colors needed to color the plane so that no single color class realizes all distances between pairs of points?

evidence.quote: Say that a set S in E2 realizes distance d if some two points x, y ∈ S are distance d apart. The polychromatic number of the plane is the least number of colors χp (E2 ) such that it is possible to color the plane with χp (E2 ) colors so that no color realizes all distances. Of course, χp (E2 ) ≤ χ(E2 ), since in the latter case no color realizes distance 1. The bounds 4 ≤ χp (E2 ) ≤ 6 are due to Stechkin and published in [21], though as with χ(E2 ), the determination of the actual number χp (E2 ) is open.

artifact.self_contained_problem: For a subset $S$ of the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{E}^2$, say that $S$ realizes a distance $d>0$ if there exist points $x,y\in S$ with $\|x-y\|=d$. Define the polychromatic number of the plane, $\chi_p(\mathbb{E}^2)$, to be the least positive integer $k$ for which there exists a partition (coloring) of $\mathbb{E}^2$ into $k$ color classes such that no single color class realizes every positive distance $d>0$. It is known that $4\le \chi_p(\mathbb{E}^2)\le 6$. Determine the exact value of $\chi_p(\mathbb{E}^2)$.

artifact.status_search_result: The polychromatic number of the plane remains unresolved. The bounds 4 ≤ χ_p(E²) ≤ 6, due to Raiskii (lower) and Stechkin (upper) around 1970, are still the best known, and the exact value has not been determined.
